queue.title: 1,800-year-old Roman toddler's grave found frozen in time, and it still had toys inside
queue.dek: A Roman child burial in the Tomis necropolis revealed clay toys, bronze amulets and flower garlands preserved for 1,800 years in an intact sarcophagus in Romania.
queue.opening: Archaeologists in Romania have unsealed an intact 1,800-year-old Roman child's sarcophagus — finding clay toys, protective amulets and preserved flower garlands buried alongside the toddler's remains. The discovery was announced by the Museum of National History and Archaeology Constanța (MINAC) in late October, with additional details released in early November by Romania's Ministry of Culture. The find was made during archaeological excavations in the city's Flămânda area, ahead of the construction of a private residential building. 7,000-YEAR-OLD BONES UNCOVERED AT CONSTRUCTION SITE IN STARTLING FIND On-site archaeologists Constantin Băjenaru and Cătălin Nopcea first spotted signs of an intact sarcophagus on Oct. 22, before unearthing it and moving it to a museum facility, according to a translated statement from the museum. It wasn't until a few days later, on Oct. 27, that conservators, archaeologists and restoration specialists at MINAC opened the stone sarcophagus — revealing a nail-free wooden coffin inside. Officials say the grave dates to between the second and third centuries A.D., and was located near an important ancient road on the northern edge of the ancient Tomis necropolis. In its statement, Romania's Ministry of Culture said the child was estimated to be between 1 and 3 years old at the time of death. queue.opening: Anthropic’s Thursday stock market debut, valued at around $1.5 trillion, is the largest in American history and, given promises made by its founders, is likely the preface to a similarly historic flood of cash into the political system. Bloomberg projects that each of Anthropic’s seven co-founders will be worth approximately $24.5 billion now that their artificial intelligence firm has gone public. Each of the seven has also pledged to give away 80% of their equity in the firm to philanthropic causes — a promise that has raised eyebrows given Anthropic’s links to a controversial moral philosophy and its history of spending big to influence elections. Effective altruism, which some of Anthropic’s early funders and employees have voiced support for, generally treats massive political and philanthropic giving as a moral obligation to prevent AI "doomsday" scenarios, such as a rogue agent working to exterminate the human race. Though the company's founders have distanced themselves from the movement, some early employees and other figures associated with Anthropic have maintained connections to its ideas, particularly its emphasis on preventing potentially catastrophic risks from artificial intelligence. Politically, this has manifested as Anthropic's leaders throwing large sums of money behind efforts to regulate AI development . queue.dek: The Milwaukee Brewers' World Series win over the Tampa Bay Rays challenges claims a salary cap would fix competitive balance in Major League Baseball.
queue.opening: Barring a miracle, we are less than two weeks away from a prolonged work stoppage in Major League Baseball . The Collective Bargaining Agreement between the 30 team owners and the MLB Players Association expires in early December, and the two sides, despite some bargaining between them, are no closer to a deal than they were when negotiations started over the summer. If anything, they might be further apart. NEW STATEMENTS FROM ROB MANFRED, MLBPA, GUARANTEE BASEBALL IS SHUT DOWN INDEFINITELY IN TWO WEEKS The disagreement stems from the creation of a salary cap, which MLB has avoided for decades, despite other sports like the NBA and NFL implementing their own cap systems years ago. Many fans have, for some inexplicable reason, come down on the side of the owners, believing that limiting what players can earn will somehow "level the playing field," as the league's propaganda campaign has claimed. While there would be a so-called "floor" under the league's proposal, it would again be far less than the cap. Meaning that the cheaper small-market teams already raking in tens of millions of dollars per year in revenue sharing would still spend as little as possible on player payroll. MLB OWNERS ARE BACK WITH A NEW SALARY CAP PROPOSAL TO SHUT DOWN SPORT EVEN AFTER BREWERS WIN WORLD SERIES If money is such a pivotal factor, the proposed ~$80 million gap would still allow teams that try to win to sign at least three or four big-name star-level players that the cheaper teams wouldn't.

The summit in Shenzhen marked the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, bringing Trump face-to-face with two of America's chief geopolitical adversaries. Washington has spent years arming Ukraine in its war against Russia, while the Pentagon has long identified China as its primary "pacing challenge" in the Indo-Pacific. Trump's scheduled press conference at noon on Friday will offer an opportunity to elaborate on what the meetings accomplished and whether the diplomatic discussions will lead to concrete agreements. queue.title: Ross Douthat: Are the Bankers or the Tech Bros Right About AI?
queue.dek: Ross Douthat on what the paranoid world understands—and misses—about artificial intelligence.
queue.opening: Just a few months ago, it seemed like today’s Anthropic IPO , expected to be the biggest in history, would consummate a marriage between the eccentric world of artificial intelligence and the ruthless realm of finance. For years AI and Wall Street had existed as profoundly different realities—one obsessed with the superhuman and utopian and speculative, the other with the immediate and material and commodifiable. But the two domains seemed to converge decisively across 2025 and the first half of 2026, especially after Claude Code made it clear that AI could really do the work of certain highly educated humans—puncturing expectations of an AI bubble and sending Wall Street’s AI valuations to new heights. Since the summer, though, the two realities have separated once again. Anthropic’s debut may help rescue the relationship, but the wedding date has been postponed. That’s not because of any want of ambition on the AI side. The latest talk in Silicon Valley is, if anything, more radical than ever , envisioning shorter timelines for superintelligence, exponentials going up and up, AI building new AI which will build new AI in a spiral that could make the next few years decisive for the human future. There are more and less measured versions of these expectations, but the assumption of continued takeoff is broadly shared across the industry. In the world of finance, though, the AI launchpad suddenly looks a lot more fragile. Read more

queue.opening: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., is leaving the door open to a potential 2028 presidential bid as speculation grows over her political future. "I think, right now, this election just happened. We got to work on getting results for people," Ocasio-Cortez told Fox News Digital when asked whether she was considering a presidential run in 2028. The self-described democratic socialist also expressed a willingness to work with President Donald Trump on key legislative priorities as Democrats prepare to take control of the House following the 2026 midterm elections. queue.title: Republicans hold lone Alaska House seat despite losing Senate, governor races
queue.dek: Rep. Nick Begich won re-election to Alaska's lone House seat after ranked-choice tabulation, a rare Republican bright spot in a Democratic wave.
queue.opening: Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, won re-election to Alaska’s lone House seat Wednesday, surviving a Democratic wave that flipped both the Senate seat and the governor’s mansion. Begich, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, defeated independent challenger Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and retired teacher backed by the Alaska Democratic Party, following the state’s ranked-choice voting tabulation. Begich’s victory, called at 9:27 p.m. ET on Wednesday – more than two weeks after Election Day – stood in sharp contrast to the rest of Alaska’s top-of-the-ticket results, where voters handed Democrats major breakthroughs despite Trump winning the state by 13% in 2024. HUNDREDS OF SUBPOENAS FLY IN DOJ’S ‘DECOY DAN’ PROBE AS DEMOCRAT PELTOLA DECLARED WINNER IN ALASKA The race was among the final House contests called nationally after the Nov. 3 general election, offering a rare bright spot for Republicans in a midterm cycle that saw Democrats seize control of both chambers of Congress. Democrats thus far hold a 257-172 majority in the House, having flipped 46 seats to just three for Republicans. There are three races that remain too close to call. "This process requires engagement, and the perspectives brought forward during the campaign added value for Alaskans as they made important decisions about their vote in this race," Begich said in a statement after his victory. queue.title: China blocks Bloomberg reporter from Trump-Putin-Xi meeting over question to Trump
queue.dek: Chinese officials barred Bloomberg's Annmarie Hordern from the meeting of President Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin after her earlier question.
queue.opening: Chinese officials barred a Bloomberg reporter from a high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin after she asked a question during an earlier bilateral session. The clash over press access unfolded on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China , where the three leaders gathered for their first-ever three-way meeting to discuss nuclear arms control, trade and the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Despite a push from the White House to get her admitted, Chinese officials refused to budge on barring Bloomberg reporter Annmarie Hordern from the room. Hordern was blocked after she called out a question to Trump during his earlier one-on-one meeting with Xi: "President Trump, has Jensen Huang been disloyal to the United States?" CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO A second reporter also started to ask a question during the bilateral session but was shushed by Chinese officials. Beijing subsequently passed along a message to the U.S. travel pool warning that yelling questions is considered "extremely rude" and that journalists would be pulled from the room if they did so. A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity surrounding the issue, said Chinese officials insisted Hordern not be allowed into the trilateral meeting even as the White House advocated for her inclusion.
